new_statements.rule_in_words: Guthrie records Luimbi's principal sound-shifts, which in his Inventory include the 'Tones' line, as broadly those of K.14 Lwena apart from listed consonant reflexes; the Lwena entry reads 'Tones: *CV1 only tonally distinct', i.e. the Proto-Bantu high/low contrast survives on the first stem syllable only. By implication Luimbi is a (reduced) tone language; nothing is said about stress, accent or penultimate length.

new_statements.identity_note: Guthrie's K.12a is Luimbi of Angola by definition of the referential classification (Glottolog luim1238 = K12a); Guthrie had first-hand Luimbi data (his 1948 Classification cites 'LUIMBI (12) aa mazi'). The tonal information is stated on the K.14 Lwena entry and carried to K.12a by Guthrie's 'Broadly similar to K.14, but..' convention, under which only the listed (segmental) shifts differ. | group-level statement: Guthrie's K.12 'Luimbi' [Angola] is Luimbi/Lwimbi [lum] (later K.12a in Guthrie 1971 and Maho 2003/2009); the prosodic remarks are stated for 'the languages of the zone' (Zone K) and single out only Ciokwe (11) and Mbunda (15) for penultimate lengthening; no Luimbi-specific data are cited in the visible text. new_statements.translation: We have not deciphered the whole tonal system of the Lwimbi language; for this reason the tones are not marked in this article. All data were transcribed phonetically using the International Phonetic Alphabet and the SIL Doulos IPA font.

new_statements.relation_note: Only the one methodological sentence presupposing a tonal system; no phonology section otherwise (classification, K12a vs K12b identity, Kimbundu/Umbundu contact features, wordlist).
new_statements.rule_in_words: The fieldworkers treat Lwimbi as having a (lexical) tonal system, which they had not yet fully analysed, so tone is left unmarked; nothing is said about stress/accent, and the 90 Lwimbi IPA forms in the table (pp. 282-287) carry no stress marks (the Brazilian Portuguese comparanda do) and no tone marks.
new_statements.identity_note: Explicitly Lwimbi K12a; data elicited 2009-2010 from three speakers (one family) from Sachinemuna, municipio do Kuemba (Cuemba), Bie province, on the Cuanza - the Luimbi area of Glottolog's coordinates; authors distinguish it from Ngangela K12b and note the local names Mbandi/Mbande. First-hand fieldwork article (etymological aim) with a 90-item IPA wordlist; the first author's PhD on Lwimbi was 'in progress' in 2010 (no record of completion found). | A's work 2 (pointer, not-attempted) now downloaded sources AND READ. The thesis describes K12b Ngangela (Nyemba cluster, glottocode nyem1238; our bibliography had it as 'not located', world-pass list of works to obtain priority high), the sister variety of Luimbi K12a inside the Ngangela group; chapter I never mentions Lwimbi/Luimbi (a full-text search for stress/accent: 0). Any use for luim1238 needs an explicit sister-variety identity note; it is NOT a Luimbi statement. The author cites and aligns with Maniacky 2002 (Menongue variety).

sources.note: Luimbi appears only as 'Lu-imbi (86 c)', a vocabulary from Fr. Keeling (p. 799). No Luimbi-specific accent remark. The front-matter transcription convention says only, for Bantu generally: 'The accent or pitch of the voice is indicated by '. This is so normally and frequently on the penultimate syllable that the accent is only employed when an exception to the prevailing rule in Bantu transfers the voice-pitch to the first, last, or other syllable than the penultimate.' -- a pan-Bantu convention, not a statement about Luimbi.
